prompt:
Determine whether there exists a differentiable function $f\colon[0,1]\to\mathbb R$ such that
$$f(0)=f(1)=1,\qquad|f'(x)|\le2\ \text{for all }x\in[0,1]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\left|\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12 .$$

solutions.title: Squeeze above $|2x-1|$
solutions.body:
Suppose such $f$ exists. For $x\in(0,1)$, the mean value theorem on $[0,x]$ gives $c\in(0,x)$ with $\frac{f(x)-1}{x}=f'(c)\ge-2$, so $f(x)\ge1-2x$. On $[x,1]$ it gives $d\in(x,1)$ with $\frac{f(x)-1}{x-1}=f'(d)\le2$; as $x-1<0$, $f(x)\ge1+2(x-1)=2x-1$. Together (also at $x=0,1$)
$$f(x)\ge|2x-1|\qquad(0\le x\le1).$$
Hence
$$\frac12=\int_0^1|2x-1|\,dx\le\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\le\left|\int_0^1f(x)\,dx\right|\le\frac12,$$
so $\int_0^1\big(f(x)-|2x-1|\big)dx=0$. The integrand is continuous ($f$ is differentiable, hence continuous) and nonnegative, so it vanishes identically: $f(x)=|2x-1|$ on $[0,1]$. But this function is not differentiable at $x=\frac12$, a contradiction.

**Answer: no, such a function does not exist.** ∎

prompt: For any given pair of positive integers $m>n$ find all $a\in\mathbb R$ for which the polynomial $x^m-ax^n+1$ can be expressed as a quotient of two nonzero polynomials with real nonnegative coefficients.
answer: Exactly the $a$ with $a<m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}=\dfrac{m}{n^{n/m}(m-n)^{(m-n)/m}}$, i.e. exactly when $x^m-ax^n+1$ has no positive root.

solutions.title: Positive roots vs. telescoping $u^K-v^K$
solutions.body:
Let $f(x)=x^m-ax^n+1$ and $a^*=m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}=\big(\tfrac mn\big)^{n/m}\big(\tfrac m{m-n}\big)^{(m-n)/m}$.

**$a\le0$ works:** $f=f/1$ has nonnegative coefficients. From now on $a>0$.

**If $a\ge a^*$, impossible.** $f'(x)=x^{n-1}(mx^{m-n}-an)$ vanishes at $x_0=(an/m)^{1/(m-n)}>0$, and
$$f(x_0)=1-x_0^n\big(a-x_0^{m-n}\big)=1-a\,\frac{m-n}{m}\,x_0^n .$$
Since $a\,x_0^n=a\big(\tfrac{an}{m}\big)^{n/(m-n)}=a^{m/(m-n)}\big(\tfrac nm\big)^{n/(m-n)}$,
$$f(x_0)\le0\iff a^{m/(m-n)}\ge\frac{m}{m-n}\Big(\frac mn\Big)^{n/(m-n)}\iff a\ge\Big(\frac m{m-n}\Big)^{(m-n)/m}\Big(\frac mn\Big)^{n/m}=a^* .$$
As $f(0)=1>0$, for $a\ge a^*$ the polynomial $f$ has a root $\beta\in(0,x_0]$. If $f=P/Q$ with nonzero $P,Q$ having nonnegative coefficients, then $P=fQ$ gives $P(\beta)=0$; but a nonzero polynomial with nonnegative coefficients is positive at every $\beta>0$. Contradiction.

**If $0<a<a^*$, possible.** For a positive integer $N$ let $K=mnN$, $u=x^m+1$, $v=ax^n$, and
$$P=u^K-v^K,\qquad Q=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}u^{K-1-j}v^j .$$
Then $P=(u-v)Q=fQ$, so $f=P/Q$, and $Q\ne0$ has nonnegative coefficients (as $a>0$). In $P=(x^m+1)^K-a^Kx^{nK}$ the only possibly negative coefficient is that of $x^{nK}=x^{m\cdot n^2N}$, which equals $\binom{K}{n^2N}-a^K$. So it suffices to find $N$ with
$$\binom{K}{k}\ge a^K,\qquad K=mnN,\ k=n^2N .$$
*Binomial estimate.* Let $\theta=k/K=n/m\in(0,1)$. In the expansion $1=(\theta+(1-\theta))^K=\sum_j\binom Kj\theta^j(1-\theta)^{K-j}$ the ratio of consecutive terms is $\frac{(K-j)k}{(j+1)(K-k)}$, which is $>1$ for $j<k$ and $<1$ for $j\ge k$; so the term $j=k$ is the largest of the $K+1$ terms and is at least $\frac1{K+1}$. Hence
$$\binom Kk\ge\frac{1}{K+1}\Big(\theta^{-\theta}(1-\theta)^{-(1-\theta)}\Big)^K=\frac{(a^*)^K}{K+1},$$
since $\theta^{-\theta}(1-\theta)^{-(1-\theta)}=(m/n)^{n/m}(m/(m-n))^{(m-n)/m}=a^*$. Because $a<a^*$ and $(K+1)^{1/K}\to1$, we get $(a^*)^K/(K+1)\ge a^K$ for all large $N$. Then $P$ has nonnegative coefficients, as required.

(The official solution reaches the same limit $\binom{K}{k}^{1/K}\to a^*$ via Stirling's formula.)

**Answer: $a<m\,n^{-n/m}(m-n)^{n/m-1}$ (all such real $a$, including all $a\le0$).** ∎

prompt:
Let $x_1,\dots,x_n$ be given real numbers with $0<m\le x_i\le M$ for each $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$. Let $X$ be the discrete random variable uniformly distributed on $\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$. The mean $\mu$ and the variance $\sigma^2$ of $X$ are defined as
$$\mu(X)=\frac{x_1+\dots+x_n}{n}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sigma^2(X)=\frac{(x_1-\mu(X))^2+\dots+(x_n-\mu(X))^2}{n}.$$
By $X^2$ denote the discrete random variable uniformly distributed on $\{x_1^2,\dots,x_n^2\}$. Prove that
$$\sigma^2(X)\ge\left(\frac{m}{2M^2}\right)^2\sigma^2(X^2).$$

solutions.title: Pairwise form of the variance
solutions.body:
For any numbers $y_1,\dots,y_n$ with mean $\bar y$,
$$\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j}(y_i-y_j)^2=\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i,j}\big(y_i^2+y_j^2-2y_iy_j\big)=2\cdot\frac1n\sum_iy_i^2-2\bar y^2=2\sigma^2(Y).$$
Apply it to $y_i=x_i^2$. Since $0<x_i,x_j\le M$,
$$(x_i^2-x_j^2)^2=(x_i+x_j)^2(x_i-x_j)^2\le4M^2(x_i-x_j)^2,$$
so
$$\sigma^2(X^2)=\frac1{2n^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_i^2-x_j^2)^2\le4M^2\cdot\frac{1}{2n^2}\sum_{i,j}(x_i-x_j)^2=4M^2\sigma^2(X).$$
Therefore, using $m\le M$,
$$\left(\frac m{2M^2}\right)^2\sigma^2(X^2)\le\frac{m^2}{4M^4}\cdot4M^2\,\sigma^2(X)=\frac{m^2}{M^2}\,\sigma^2(X)\le\sigma^2(X).$$
∎ (The proved inequality $\sigma^2(X)\ge\frac{1}{4M^2}\sigma^2(X^2)$ is even stronger than required.)

solutions.title: Variance as a minimum
solutions.body:
For any random variable $Y$ and constant $c$, $\mathbb E(Y-c)^2=\sigma^2(Y)+(\mathbb EY-c)^2\ge\sigma^2(Y)$. Take $Y=X^2$ and $c=\mu^2$ with $\mu=\mu(X)\in[m,M]$:
$$\sigma^2(X^2)\le\mathbb E\big(X^2-\mu^2\big)^2=\mathbb E\big[(X+\mu)^2(X-\mu)^2\big]\le(2M)^2\,\mathbb E(X-\mu)^2=4M^2\sigma^2(X).$$
As in the first solution, $\frac{m^2}{4M^4}\sigma^2(X^2)\le\frac{m^2}{M^2}\sigma^2(X)\le\sigma^2(X)$. ∎

prompt:
A function $f\colon\mathbb Z^+\to\mathbb R$ is called multiplicative if for every $a,b\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$ we have $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)$. Let $g$ be the multiplicative function given by
$$g(p^\alpha)=\alpha p^{\alpha-1},$$
where $\alpha\in\mathbb Z^+$ and $p>0$ is a prime. Prove that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that
$$g(n)+1=g(n+1).$$
answer: $g(13^2)=26$, $g(3^3)=27$ and $g=1$ on squarefree numbers; take $n=169x$, $n+1=27y$ with $x=77+1053t$, $y=482+6591t$ squarefree, which happens for a positive proportion of $t$ (e.g. $n=13013$).

solutions.title: Two prime powers and squarefree values of linear forms
solutions.body:
**Values of $g$.** For a squarefree $x=p_1\cdots p_r$, $g(x)=\prod g(p_i)=\prod 1\cdot p_i^0=1$. Also $g(13^2)=2\cdot13=26$ and $g(3^3)=3\cdot3^2=27$. Hence, by multiplicativity,
$$g(169x)=26\ \text{ if $x$ is squarefree and }13\nmid x,\qquad g(27y)=27\ \text{ if $y$ is squarefree and }3\nmid y .$$
So it suffices to find infinitely many such pairs with $169x+1=27y$; then $n=169x$ satisfies $g(n)+1=27=g(n+1)$.

**A family of solutions.** $169\cdot77+1=13014=27\cdot482$, and for $t\ge0$ put
$$x_t=77+1053t,\qquad y_t=482+6591t\qquad(1053=27\cdot39,\ 6591=169\cdot39).$$
Then $169x_t+1=13014+177957t=27y_t$. Moreover $x_t\equiv77\equiv12\pmod{13}$ and $y_t\equiv482\equiv2\pmod3$, so $13\nmid x_t$ and $3\nmid y_t$; also $x_t\equiv2\pmod 3$ and $y_t\equiv1\pmod{13}$. (For $t=0$: $x_0=77=7\cdot11$, $y_0=482=2\cdot241$ are squarefree, giving $g(13013)=26$, $g(13014)=27$.)

**Infinitely many $t$ with $x_t,y_t$ both squarefree.** Fix a large $X$ and count $t\in\{0,1,\dots,X-1\}$ for which $p^2\mid x_t$ or $p^2\mid y_t$ for some prime $p$.
- $p=3$ and $p=13$ never occur, by the congruences above.
- For $p\notin\{3,13\}$, $p\nmid1053\cdot6591=3^5\cdot13^4$, so $p^2\mid x_t$ holds for $t$ in a single residue class modulo $p^2$; the number of such $t<X$ is at most $X/p^2+1$. The same holds for $y_t$.
- Only primes with $p^2\le y_{X-1}<6591X$, i.e. $p<\sqrt{6591X}$, can occur.

Hence the number of bad $t$ is at most
$$\sum_{p<\sqrt{6591X},\ p\ne3,13}2\Big(\frac X{p^2}+1\Big)\le2X\Big(\frac14+\sum_{k\ge5\ \text{odd}}\frac1{k^2}\Big)+2\sqrt{6591X}.$$
Since $\sum_{k\ \text{odd}}\frac1{k^2}=\frac{\pi^2}8$, the bracket equals $\frac14+\frac{\pi^2}8-1-\frac19<0.373$. So at least $0.254X-2\sqrt{6591X}$ values $t<X$ are good, and this tends to infinity with $X$.

Each good $t$ gives $n=169x_t$ with $g(n)+1=g(n+1)$, and different $t$ give different $n$. ∎

(The official solution uses a theorem of Prachar on the density of squarefree numbers in arithmetic progressions; the elementary count above suffices.)
